[LLM] Grandoreiro WebRTC/STUN C2 from non-conferencing process Command & Control Medium
Hunts outbound STUN/TURN traffic (UDP/TCP 3478/3479/5349/5350) initiated by a process running from a user-writable path that is NOT a known web-conferencing or browser app. WatchGuard reports Grandoreiro's sgcWebSockets-based DLLs hide C2 inside WebRTC/STUN to blend with conferencing traffic. Rationale: Targets the WatchGuard-reported STUN/WebRTC C2 channel (ports 3478/5349) but anchors fidelity on the initiating process: a binary in a user-writable path that isn't a browser/conferencing app talking STUN is anomalous. Sentinel variant lacks the initiating-process pivot (ImNetworkSession has no process field) so it is lower-fidelity and best used for triage. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/grandoreiro-malware-and-btmob-rat.html • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0531/
ATT&CKT1572 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort in (3478, 3479, 5349, 5350)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("teams.exe","ms-teams.exe","msteams.exe","zoom.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","slack.exe","webex.exe","skype.exe","discord.exe","whatsapp.exe","outlook.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Public\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Connections = count(), DistinctDest = dcount(RemoteIP), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemotePort
| order by Connections desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber in (3478, 3479, 5349, 5350)
| summarize Connections = count(), DistinctDst = dcount(DstIpAddr) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol
| order by Connections desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent

AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

[LLM] Node/npm postinstall recursively reading Claude /mnt/user-data artifacts Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a node or npm process enumerating and reading many files under Anthropic Claude's /mnt/user-data upload/output directory — the collection step of the Malware-Slop stealer before it ships them to GitHub. Anchors on the article-specific path and the install-time process context. Rationale: Uses the article-named directory /mnt/user-data (Claude's upload/output workspace) plus node/npm process context, mirroring the malware's 'structured synchronization of local workspace files'. The dcount>=5 threshold separates the recursive theft sweep from incidental single-file touches. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/malicious-npm-package-stole-files-from.html • https://www.ox.security/blog/npm-packages-compromised/
ATT&CKT1005 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath startswith "/mnt/user-data"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node","sh")
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), Files = make_set(FileName, 25),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
        by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where FileCount >= 5   // recursive collection of multiple Claude artifacts, not a single file touch
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/mnt/user-data"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm")
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), Files = make_set(TargetFileName, 25),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
        by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where FileCount >= 5
| order by LastSeen desc

| FileCount >= 5

[LLM] Claude /mnt/user-data collection followed by node/npm egress to GitHub API Actions on Objectives High
Correlates the collection step (node/npm reading /mnt/user-data) with an outbound connection to GitHub (api.github.com / github.com / uploads.github.com) from the same host within 10 minutes — the Malware-Slop exfiltration-to-code-repository chain. The temporal join makes ordinary github.com traffic from build tooling high-fidelity only when it immediately follows a Claude-artifact sweep. Rationale: Joins the two confirmed behaviours from the OX write-up — reading /mnt/user-data and uploading to a GitHub account via the API — into one temporal correlation, so benign node→github.com traffic only alerts when it directly follows a Claude-artifact collection sweep. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/malicious-npm-package-stole-files-from.html • https://www.ox.security/blog/npm-packages-compromised/ • https://www.tipranks.com/news/private-companies/ox-security-highlights-emerging-npm-malware-threat-to-ci-pipelines-and-ai-developer-tools

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Filesystem

DeviceNetworkEvents

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

            - '\mshta.exe'

            - '\regsvr32.exe'

level: high

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Post-takedown beacon to CrowdStrike Glassworm sinkhole 164.92.88.210 Command & Control High
Hunts any outbound connection from a developer endpoint to CrowdStrike's announced sinkhole IP 164.92.88.210. Per the article, every still-infected Glassworm host beacons to this address post-disruption, making it a near-zero-FP confirmed-infection indicator. Rationale: 164.92.88.210 is CrowdStrike's named sinkhole — the article explicitly says all still-infected machines now beacon here, making any hit a confirmed legacy Glassworm infection. Cross-checked CrowdStrike's own write-up referenced in the article and the Shadowserver Foundation sinkhole pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/ • https://www.shadowserver.org/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "164.92.88.210"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "164.92.88.210" or SourceIP == "164.92.88.210"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Outbound connection to Glassworm operator VPS C2 infrastructure Command & Control High
Hunts outbound connections from any endpoint to the four operator-controlled VPS IPs Glassworm used for direct C2 / payload delivery. These remain valuable because retrospective searches reveal which dev workstations were infected before the takedown. Rationale: These four IPs are listed in the article's pre-extracted IOC block as the direct-server C2 layer beneath the Solana/BitTorrent/Calendar resolution dance. Exact-match IP hunting is the highest-fidelity pivot available against Glassworm. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/ • https://www.shadowserver.org/

[LLM] VS Code / Node / Cursor process resolving Solana mainnet RPC (Glassworm C2 channel) Command & Control Medium
Hunts developer-IDE / node processes resolving or connecting to api.mainnet-beta.solana.com and other Solana RPC endpoints — the article describes GlasswormRAT pulling C2 addresses from Solana memo fields. Legitimate Solana RPC traffic from a non-wallet, non-blockchain-dev workstation is anomalous. Rationale: The article explicitly names Solana blockchain memos as one of the four resolution layers; api.mainnet-beta.solana.com is the default Solana RPC endpoint. Limiting parent-process to dev IDEs (Code.exe / node.exe / cursor.exe / electron.exe) keeps the FP rate sane because real Solana developers do exist. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.solana.com/cluster/rpc-endpoints • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/001/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("mainnet-beta.solana.com", "solana-api.projectserum.com", "api.devnet.solana.com", "rpc.ankr.com/solana", ".solana.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","node.exe","cursor.exe","code - insiders.exe","electron.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let SolanaHosts = dynamic(["api.mainnet-beta.solana.com","solana-api.projectserum.com","api.devnet.solana.com"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (SolanaHosts) or Name endswith ".solana.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Developer endpoint emitting BitTorrent DHT bootstrap traffic from non-torrent process Command & Control High
Hunts for UDP traffic to BitTorrent DHT bootstrap nodes (router.bittorrent.com, dht.transmissionbt.com, router.utorrent.com) originating from VS Code / Node / Cursor processes. The article names BitTorrent DHT as one of Glassworm's four C2 resolution channels — legitimate developer workstations should never have an IDE process querying the DHT. Rationale: BitTorrent DHT is the second of Glassworm's four C2 channels per the article. DHT traffic from a code-editor process tree is extremely abnormal — torrent clients run as their own binaries, never embedded inside VS Code. Cross-checked the BitTorrent DHT BEP-0005 bootstrap routers list. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bittorrent.org/beps/bep_0005.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/002/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","node.exe","cursor.exe","electron.exe","code - insiders.exe")
| where (RemoteUrl has_any (DhtBootstrap)) or (Protocol == "Udp" and RemotePort between (6881 .. 6889))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc

DnsEvents

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] IDE / Node process resolving calendar.google.com as Glassworm C2 dead-drop Command & Control Medium
Hunts for non-browser developer-tool processes (Code.exe, node.exe, cursor.exe, electron.exe) making DNS or HTTPS calls to calendar.google.com / googleapis.com calendar endpoints. Glassworm uses Google Calendar event titles as Base64-encoded C2 dead-drop locations — legitimate IDEs do not hit the Calendar API. Rationale: Article explicitly states 'Glassworm uses Google Calendar event titles as dead-drop locations for Base64-encoded C2 paths'. Scoping the parent process to VS Code / Node keeps FP rate manageable since legitimate calendar use happens in browsers, not IDEs. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/001/ • https://developers.google.com/calendar/api/v3/reference

[LLM] Trojanized Glassworm VS Code / OpenVSX extension package files on developer host Installation High
Hunts for file-write events under %USERPROFILE%\.vscode\extensions or ~/.vscode-server matching the eight Glassworm-trojanized extension package names. Any installation directory containing these is a confirmed compromise indicator regardless of network telemetry. Rationale: The kill-chain block enumerates exactly eight package names as Glassworm IOCs. Any file write under .vscode/extensions matching one of these is a confirmed install of a trojanized package — there is no benign overlap with these specific names. Confirmed via CrowdStrike's disclosure referenced in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/ • https://open-vsx.org/

[LLM] VS Code child process reads wallet / dev-credential files (Glassworm credential theft) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for Code.exe / node.exe / electron.exe (or their child processes) reading high-value credential or wallet files within seconds of an extension directory write — the article describes trojanized extensions harvesting cryptocurrency wallets and developer credentials. Rationale: Article: 'stole cryptocurrency wallets and developer credentials'. Combines the IDE-process predicate (Glassworm runs inside the extension host) with the canonical credential / wallet file paths — both halves are documented in the article's kill-chain block. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/ • https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/metamask/nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn

[LLM] First-time install of any Glassworm-named extension across the org (baseline anti-join) Delivery Medium
Surfaces the first organisation-wide installation of any of the eight named Glassworm extension package names. Defenders who haven't yet hit Glassworm get an early-warning signal as soon as a developer pulls a re-uploaded clone. Designed for environments where IOC names may resurface under typosquatted variants. Rationale: The eight package names are explicit Glassworm IOCs from the kill-chain block. Baseline anti-join means SOC only sees a host the *first* time it picks up a trojanized extension — avoids alert fatigue once a host is already known-compromised. Sigma omitted because anti-join over baseline is a correlation, not single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://open-vsx.org/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1176

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] SRG/Luna Moth typosquatted IT-helpdesk lookalike domain resolution · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SRG in-person USB exfil: mass file copy to non-system drive after remote-help tool · [LLM] SRG extortion leak-site contact: traffic to business-data-leaks.com · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] SRG/Luna Moth typosquatted IT-helpdesk lookalike domain resolution Delivery High
Surfaces DNS resolution or HTTP traffic from any corporate endpoint to the SRG/Luna Moth typosquatted helpdesk lookalike domains named in the May 2026 FBI flash alert. Rationale: Domains pulled verbatim from the article IOC list (duanemorris-helpdesk.com, perkinscoie-helpdesk.com, millermartin-helpdesk.com). [LLM] SRG in-person USB exfil: mass file copy to non-system drive after remote-help tool Actions on Objectives Medium
Catches the SRG fallback playbook — when the phone-based remote-desktop attempt fails, an SRG operative shows up in person and copies data via USB/external HDD. Looks for a burst of file writes to a non-C: drive shortly after a known remote-help binary executed on the same host. Rationale: Article explicitly states: 'SRG sends a threat actor to the victim's location to gain access to insert a storage device into the victim's computer' and 'steal data by connecting USB drives or external hard drives'. The remote-help tool list comes from EclecticIQ + prior FBI PIN documentation of Luna Moth's preferred RMM tooling (Zoho Assist, AnyDesk, Splashtop, Atera, Syncro). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/luna-moth-callback-phishing-campaign-targets-us-legal-and-financial-firms • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-warns-silent-ransom-group-targets-law-firms-in-callback-phishing-attacks/

[LLM] SRG extortion leak-site contact: traffic to business-data-leaks.com Actions on Objectives High
Detects any outbound contact from a corporate endpoint to the SRG/Luna Moth public leak site business-data-leaks.com. A hit means either a victim navigating to verify a ransom threat, or an SRG-controlled host inside the network signalling/posting. Rationale: business-data-leaks.com is named in the article as the SRG-controlled leak site used to extort victims. Any outbound hit from a corp host is presumptively malicious or victim-impact-stage — extremely low base rate. Cross-checked with the May 2025 FBI PIN and EclecticIQ writeup which both reference Luna Moth's data-leak-site model. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/luna-moth-callback-phishing-campaign-targets-us-legal-and-financial-firms • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-warns-silent-ransom-group-targets-law-firms-in-callback-phishing-attacks/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657/

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain

status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GlassWorm Malware Takedown Disrupts Developer Supply Chain Attack Infrastructure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] VS Code / Cursor child writes to Chrome extension directory (GlassWormRAT browser extension drop) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GlassWorm direct-VPS C2 IP egress (217.69.3.218 / 199.247.10.166 / 140.82.52.31 / 199.247.13.106) · [LLM] Solana mainnet RPC queried by VS Code / Cursor / Node.js (dead-drop resolver) · [LLM] Google Calendar API dead-drop polled by code-editor / Node process · [LLM] BitTorrent DHT bootstrap traffic from developer workstation · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Developer credential & wallet file read by suspicious code-editor child · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] GlassWorm direct-VPS C2 IP egress (217.69.3.218 / 199.247.10.166 / 140.82.52.31 / 199.247.13.106) Command & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the four commercial-VPS C2 endpoints CrowdStrike/Shadowserver attributed to GlassWorm — one of the four resilient channels used by the JS RAT to receive instructions and exfil developer tokens. Article-specific because these IPs only appear in GlassWorm reporting. Rationale: Pre-extracted IOC list names exactly these four IPs; CrowdStrike's takedown writeup is the only public source citing them as GlassWorm direct C2, so any single hit is investigation-worthy regardless of process context.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let GlassWormC2 = dynamic(["217.69.3.218","199.247.10.166","140.82.52.31","199.247.13.106"]);
ImNetworkSession

| where DstIpAddr in (GlassWormC2)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Solana mainnet RPC queried by VS Code / Cursor / Node.js (dead-drop resolver) Command & Control Medium
Hunts the GlassWorm Solana-blockchain dead-drop resolver: the malware queries Solana mainnet RPC endpoints to read C2 server addresses from memo fields of blockchain transactions. Article-specific because Solana RPC traffic from a code editor or its node.exe child is not legitimate developer behaviour outside Web3 teams. Rationale: Article explicitly names the Solana blockchain as the first of four C2 dead-drop channels — RPC queries to api.mainnet-beta.solana.com from a VS Code fork or its Node.js child is the exact behavioural footprint of the resolver fetching memo-field C2 addresses. Solana RPC hostnames are well documented in Solana's public docs.

[LLM] VS Code / Cursor child writes to Chrome extension directory (GlassWormRAT browser extension drop) Installation High
Hunts the secondary GlassWormRAT stage that installs a Google Chrome extension to harvest screenshots, keystrokes, and clipboard. The article specifies a code-editor-spawned process installs the Chrome extension, so writes into Chrome's Extensions folder by a non-Chrome process originating from a VS Code fork are the exact drop pattern. Rationale: Article states the RAT "install[s] a Google Chrome extension that, in turn, collects sensitive data, including screenshots, keystrokes, and clipboard content." Chrome unpacked-extension folders are only legitimately written by chrome.exe itself or by the Chrome Web Store updater — writes from a Node.js / code-editor child are an exact behavioural match for the GlassWormRAT browser-extension drop.
ATT&CKT1176 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Extensions\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\Default\Extensions\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default\Extensions\", @"\Chromium\User Data\Default\Extensions\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (CodeProcs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where ActingProcessName has_any (CodeProcs)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Google Calendar API dead-drop polled by code-editor / Node process Command & Control Medium
Hunts the GlassWorm C2 channel that fetches the live C2 server address from Google Calendar event titles. Code editors and their Node.js helpers do not legitimately call the Calendar API — direct calls to calendar-v3 endpoints from these processes match the dead-drop fetch pattern. Rationale: Article explicitly states "Employing Google Calendar as a dead drop to fetch the C2 server address from event titles." Code editors / Node have no business calling the Calendar v3 API; the call is the resolver. Excluding fonts/storage googleapis paths removes the obvious legitimate Google traffic.
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevEditors)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("calendar.google.com","googleapis.com/calendar","www.googleapis.com")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

[LLM] Developer credential & wallet file read by suspicious code-editor child Actions on Objectives High
Hunts the GlassWorm credential-harvesting stage that searches the host for GitHub / npm / OpenVSX tokens and crypto-wallet files. Reads of these specific secret paths by a Node / Python / PowerShell child of a code editor match Endor Labs' description of the searcher. Rationale: Endor Labs is quoted verbatim: "the malware searches the host for developer credentials (GitHub, NPM, OpenVSX tokens, crypto wallets)". Reading `\.config\gh\hosts.yml`, `.npmrc`, `.openvsx`, `.vsce`, and the named wallet directories from a code-editor-spawned child within a short window is precisely the searcher's footprint; requiring ≥2 distinct secret paths suppresses incidental single-file reads.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let SecretPaths = dynamic([@"\.npmrc", @"\.config\gh\hosts.yml", @"\AppData\Roaming\Exodus\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Electrum\wallets", @"\AppData\Roaming\Solana\", @"\AppData\Local\Coinbase Wallet\", @"\.openvsx\", @"\.vsce\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Code\User\globalStorage\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Cursor\User\globalStorage\", @"\.ssh\id_rsa", @"\.ssh\id_ed25519", @"wallet.dat", @"keystore"]);
let ChildProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","python.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","electron.exe"]);
let EditorParents = dynamic(["code.exe","cursor.exe","windsurf.exe","positron.exe","vscodium.exe"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
   or (isnotempty(FolderPath))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (ChildProcs)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (EditorParents)
| where FolderPath has_any (SecretPaths) or FileName in~ (".npmrc","wallet.dat","id_rsa","id_ed25519")
| summarize SecretsTouched=dcount(FolderPath), SamplePaths=make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where SecretsTouched >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
let SecretPaths = dynamic([@"\.npmrc", @"\.config\gh\hosts.yml", @"\AppData\Roaming\Exodus\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Electrum\wallets", @"\AppData\Roaming\Solana\", @"\AppData\Local\Coinbase Wallet\", @"\.openvsx\", @"\.vsce\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Code\User\globalStorage\", @"\.ssh\id_rsa", @"wallet.dat"]);
let ChildProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","python.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","electron.exe"]);
let EditorParents = dynamic(["code.exe","cursor.exe","windsurf.exe","positron.exe","vscodium.exe"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any (ChildProcs)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (SecretPaths) or TargetFileName in~ (".npmrc","wallet.dat","id_rsa","id_ed25519")
| summarize SecretsTouched=dcount(TargetFilePath), SamplePaths=make_set(TargetFilePath, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where SecretsTouched >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.config\\gh\\hosts.yml OR *\\Exodus\\* OR *\\Electrum\\wallets\\* OR *\\Solana\\* OR *\\Coinbase\ Wallet\\* OR *\\.openvsx\\* OR *\\.vsce\\* OR *\\.ssh\\id_rsa OR *\\.ssh\\id_ed25519 OR *\\wallet.dat) @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\electron.exe) @ParentImage:(*\\code.exe OR *\\Code.exe OR *\\cursor.exe OR *\\Cursor.exe OR *\\windsurf.exe OR *\\vscodium.exe OR *\\positron.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/(\.npmrc|\\gh\\hosts\.yml|\\Exodus\\|\\Electrum\\wallets|\\Solana\\|Coinbase Wallet|\.openvsx|\.vsce|\.ssh\\id_(rsa|ed25519)|wallet\.dat)/i ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|python|powershell|pwsh|electron)\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(code|cursor|windsurf|positron|vscodium)\.exe$/i}, field=[aid, ContextProcessId=TargetProcessId])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
